n: When Ish-bosheth hears that Abner is dead, he loses all courage, and the northern tribes are thrown into alarm. Without Abner, Saul’s house has no strong leader left.

f.g: An idiom for losing heart or courage.

n: Two of Ish-bosheth’s own officers are introduced — brothers from Beeroth, a town in Benjamin. They were from Saul’s tribe, making their coming betrayal even darker.

f.g: Originally one of the Gibeonite towns, later counted as part of Benjamin.

n: A side note explains that the original people of Beeroth had fled to Gittaim and still lived there as foreigners when this account was written.

f.g: Sojourners = temporary residents, people living away from their homeland.
Until the time the narrator was writing.

n: The narrator introduces Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, who was crippled as a little boy when his nurse dropped him while fleeing after Saul’s death. He is the last real heir of Saul’s line, and he will reappear in chapter 9.

f.g: Called Merib-baal in 1 Chronicles 8:34; like Ish-bosheth, “bosheth” (shame) seems to replace “baal.”
The valley where Saul’s last battle took place.

n: The brothers come to Ish-bosheth’s house during the hottest part of the day, when he is taking his noonday rest.

f.g: In the Near East people often rested during the midday heat.

n: Pretending to collect wheat — perhaps as officers drawing supplies — they get inside and stab him.

f.g: In the belly; the same phrase used for the deaths of Asahel and Abner (2 Samuel 2:23; 3:27).

n: They kill Ish-bosheth in his bed, cut off his head, and travel all night through the Jordan valley toward Hebron.

f.g: Hebrew Arabah — the Jordan Rift Valley.

n: Expecting a reward, they present the head to David and claim God has avenged him on Saul’s family. They even try to speak in religious terms to justify murder.
David answers with a solemn oath, invoking the God who has rescued him from every danger. David did not need assassins; the Lord had always been his deliverer.

f.w: redeemed my soul out of all adversity

n: David reminds them of the Amalekite who claimed to have killed Saul and expected a reward — and was executed instead.
If that man deserved death, how much more do men who murdered an innocent man asleep in his own bed? David calls Ish-bosheth “righteous” — not guilty of any crime deserving death.

f.w: require his blood of your hand
f.g: Hold you accountable for his death.

n: The murderers are executed and their bodies publicly displayed as a warning. David gives Ish-bosheth’s head an honorable burial in Abner’s tomb, again showing respect for Saul’s house.
